title: SCHOOLED: The Bipartisan Opt-In Chorus Grows Louder
author: Petrilli, Mike
summary: Mike Petrilli's SCHOOLED digest for May 15, 2026 centers on the growing bipartisan momentum behind President Trump's Education Freedom Tax Credit (EFTC), featuring guest commentary from Chad Aldeman, Brenda Dickhoner, Jason Riley, and Colin Pascal, all supporting blue-state participation. Petrilli also covers ICE enforcement near schools (Stern and Anello arguing schools should be sanctuary spaces), teacher accountability politics (Bagley and Gordon arguing Democrats should embrace firing ineffective teachers as a winning electoral issue), and new school-choice spending data (Lueken and Ritter showing 20 years of federal data finds no per-pupil spending collapse in choice states). Naomi Schaefer Riley's critical review of Deborah Kenny's 'The Well-Educated Child' raises concerns about HVA's embrace of discovery-based math pedagogy despite adverse evidence. Petrilli also highlights demographic headwinds: Texas lost 76,000 public school students in one year, tracking nationwide enrollment decline that will require proactive consolidation planning. The digest closes with Aldeman's case for reading retention policies as behavioral levers that change adult conduct even when few children are actually retained.
points: Aldeman's key argument: the only legitimate reason for a blue state to opt out of the EFTC is to block private schools; if the goal is helping all children, opting in is the rational choice, especially given EFTC funds can flow to public school tutoring and enrichment.

Twenty years of federal data show per-pupil expenditures in choice states actually increased after choice program adoption -- directly undercutting the primary political argument against choice programs.

Research on reading retention laws shows they change adult behavior even in districts where essentially no students are actually retained: the law's value is in prompting teachers, administrators, and parents to act earlier and more intensively.

Texas public school enrollment fell 76,000 students in a single year -- the first non-pandemic decline in nearly four decades -- reflecting a structural demographic shift that will force proactive school consolidation regardless of policy choices.

Bagley and Gordon identify teacher accountability as the third most effective issue for winning swing voters (ahead of transgender sports policy and immigration positioning), yet Democrats spend vastly more political capital on the latter than the former.
quotes: The only reason to opt out is to stop private schools. But if your goal is to help kids, full stop, you should be willing to opt in. And if public school advocates get their act together and start SGOs, they could drive real resources to the kids they say they care about. [Chad Aldeman]

Ms. Hochul is up for re-election this year and waited to opt into the federal scholarship program until after her primary opponent dropped out of the race. That isn't exactly a profile in courage, but it does suggest that some Democrats in big blue states are coming around to the view that spurning federal dollars while pushing for tax increases is a bad look. [Jason Riley]

In the five years before choice, average real per pupil expenditures among choice states hovered between about $15,800 and $16,100 per student. In the year before launch, average real PPE was $15,895. It rose to $16,032 in the launch year and $16,664 five years later -- an increase of about $769 per pupil, or 4.8 percent.

Retention is not the goal of the retention policy.... The goal is for students to be identified early and receive the tutoring, the attention, the individualized reading plan to prevent a student from being retained. [Kymyona Burk, Mississippi literacy director]

A fixed, public promotion standard is one of the most effective tools we've found to change the actions of adults. Retention policy may or may not be effective for the kids who repeat a grade, but it is very effective in getting adults -- teachers, administrators, even parents -- to focus their attention and change their behavior. [Todd Collins]

She doesn't like it when teachers explain how to do something first -- let's say a math problem -- and then ask the students to do it themselves. This sounds great, but as my American Enterprise Institute colleague Daniel Buck has pointed out, this approach has been disastrous for student achievement and motivation. These struggle sessions lead students to learn less -- particularly students for whom math does not come naturally -- and persuade them they're bad at it. [Naomi Schaefer Riley on Kenny / HVA]

How many millions more words have Democrats spoken on gender rights than teacher accountability over the last year? That gap exists because getting crosswise with teachers unions is more politically costly than fighting with gender-equity groups.

The Texas decline reflects nationwide demographic changes already driving budget shortfalls, layoffs, and school closures around the country. It's time to follow Cleveland's lead and prepare communities for the challenges ahead.
